---
engine: markdown
title: "Delimited text (CSV/TSV)"
---

```{term}
#| include: false
rush run -o mtcars.csv 'mtcars'
```

CSV is the default format, for reading and for writing. Files ending in `.tsv`
are read and written with tabs, and so is standard output with `-O tsv`.

## Terminal and pipe

When the output is a terminal, `rush` prints a data frame as a table, so
that you can read it:

```{term}
rush run 'head(df, 3)' mtcars.csv
```

When the output is a file or another command, `rush` writes CSV, so that
the next tool can read it. Here, `cat` shows what `rush` writes:

```{term}
rush run 'head(df, 3)' mtcars.csv | cat
```

The options below change what is written, so most examples on this page end
with `| cat`.

## Delimiters

### `--delimiter` (`-d`)

Set the delimiter for both reading and writing. For example, to read a
semicolon-separated file and write one:

```{term}
#| include: false
rush run -D ';' -o semicolons.csv 'head(df, 3)' mtcars.csv
```

```{term}
cat semicolons.csv
rush run -d ';' 'dplyr::select(df, mpg, cyl)' semicolons.csv | cat
```

### `--input-delimiter`

Set only the input delimiter, and keep writing CSV:

```{term}
rush run --input-delimiter ';' 'dplyr::select(df, mpg, cyl)' semicolons.csv |
  cat
```

### `--output-delimiter` (`-D`)

Set only the output delimiter:

```{term}
rush run -D '|' 'head(df, 3)' mtcars.csv | cat
```

Use `$'\t'` (in bash and zsh) to pass a tab, or `-O tsv`, which is easier to
type.

## TSV

Files ending in `.tsv` are read and written with tabs:

```{term}
rush convert -o mtcars.tsv mtcars.csv
head -3 mtcars.tsv
rush run 'nrow(df)' mtcars.tsv
```

## Formats

### `--input-format` (`-F`)

Read a file as CSV regardless of its extension. This is also the default for
extensions that `rush` doesn't know:

```{term}
cp mtcars.csv mtcars.txt
rush run -F csv 'nrow(df)' mtcars.txt
```

### `--output-format` (`-O`)

Write a specific format to standard output. Unlike the default, an explicit
`-O` is used in the terminal too:

```{term}
rush run -O tsv 'head(df, 3)' mtcars.csv
```

## Headers

### `--no-header` (`-H`)

Read a file without a header row, and write without one. The columns are
named `x1`, `x2`, and so on:

```{term}
printf '1,Alice\n2,Bob\n3,Carol\n' | rush run -H 'dplyr::filter(df, x1 > 1)' -
```

### `--no-input-header`

Read a file without a header row, but write one:

```{term}
printf '1,Alice\n2,Bob\n3,Carol\n' | rush run --no-input-header 'df' - | cat
```

### `--no-output-header`

Read the header as usual, but write without one:

```{term}
rush run --no-output-header 'head(df, 3)' mtcars.csv | cat
```

### `--names`

Name the columns of a file without a header row (this implies
`--no-input-header`):

```{term}
printf '1,Alice\n2,Bob\n3,Carol\n' | rush run --names id,name 'df' - | cat
```

### `--no-clean-names` (`-C`)

`rush` cleans column names with
[`janitor::clean_names()`](https://sfirke.github.io/janitor/reference/clean_names.html),
so they are easy to use in R: lowercase, with underscores. Use `-C` to keep
the original names:

```{term}
printf 'First Name,Score (%%)\nAlice,92\n' | rush run 'names(df)' -
printf 'First Name,Score (%%)\nAlice,92\n' | rush run -C 'names(df)' -
```

## Limiting rows with `--head`

Write only the first rows of the result:

```{term}
rush run --head 3 'df' mtcars.csv | cat
```

This works for any output format, and with `rush sql` and `rush convert`:

```{term}
rush sql --head 3 "SELECT mpg, cyl FROM mtcars ORDER BY mpg DESC" mtcars.csv
```

```{term}
#| include: false
rm -f mtcars.csv mtcars.tsv mtcars.txt semicolons.csv
```
